primary_cause: Macro COVID risk-off not a fresh Merck headline. No meaningful Merck-specific negative in prior 3 days. White House death projection of 100K-240K and weak payroll and manufacturing data drove broad selloff
secondary_factors: Fear that reduced office visits and procedure volumes would hit pharma demand especially administered therapies
store_description: Merck 4.1% drop looks mostly like a defensive-stock selloff in a session when the major indexes fell more than 4% after the White House projected 100K-240K U.S. deaths and ADP showed March private payrolls down 27K. The best fundamental explanation is that investors were beginning to price in the demand hit from reduced physician visits.

primary_cause: Fear that postponed elective procedures would crush Medtronic higher-margin core device business. Medtronic on March 30 shared ventilator design specs but elective surgeries across U.S. were being postponed which was the much larger earnings issue
secondary_factors: April 1 macro selloff. Investors likely fading ventilator headlines because ventilators were too small a piece of MDT to offset procedure losses
store_description: Medtronic fell even though it had favorable COVID-related PR on March 30 around opening up PB560 ventilator specifications. The more important number was not ventilator output but the industry-wide collapse in elective procedures which hospitals were postponing to free beds and PPE hitting Medtronic much larger surgical and implant businesses.

primary_cause: Rising credit-loss and recession fears for large banks. No fresh JPM-specific negative release in prior 3 days. Key overhang already known including March 15 suspension of buybacks ahead of expected reserve build
secondary_factors: Prior suspension of buybacks. Sensitivity to unemployment and GDP assumptions
store_description: JPM 6.3% drop was primarily a bank-beta reaction to worse recession signals not a new JPM headline. With stocks down broadly after White House grim death forecast and ADP 27K March job loss print investors likely marked up expected loan-loss provisions and consumer credit stress.

primary_cause: STOCK-SPECIFIC. Visa disclosed on March 30 that transaction volumes fell in second half of March and cross-border travel spending deteriorated rapidly. Mastercard had essentially same business exposure so Visa statement was direct negative read-through
secondary_factors: Broad April 1 risk-off. Weakness in restaurants entertainment and fuel spending
store_description: The most likely driver was the March 30 read-through from Visa which said transaction volumes were falling in late March and cross-border travel-related spend was deteriorating rapidly. Because Mastercard economics are similarly exposed to travel and cross-border card fees the market repriced MA lower as those high-margin revenue streams suddenly looked much worse.

primary_cause: Renewed selling in cyclical semiconductor equipment on COVID shutdown risk and guidance uncertainty. Lam had withdrawn third-quarter guidance on March 17. No fresher Lam-specific negative headline in prior 3 days
secondary_factors: Factory contraction and recession data on April 1
store_description: Lam 6.9% decline appears to have been an extension of the semicap de-rating that followed its March guidance withdrawal rather than a brand-new company event. Once March 31-April 1 data reinforced that the economy was slipping sharply investors likely leaned harder against equipment makers whose customers could delay capex.

primary_cause: Market fear that retail demand and margins would be hit by lockdowns despite essential status. Lowe's announced March 25 it would hire roughly 30K workers and commit $100M in pandemic response measures implying higher near-term costs
secondary_factors: Extra labor and cost commitments from pandemic response. April 1 recession selloff
store_description: Lowe's had just committed to about 30K hires and $100M of support measures which strengthened operations but also signaled rising cost pressure. On April 1 with payroll and manufacturing data worsening investors likely looked through near-term DIY demand support and focused on margin risk plus the chance of broader home-improvement traffic disruption.

primary_cause: Recession-driven expectations for industrial demand destruction. No fresh Linde-specific negative headline in prior 3 days. Industrial gases exposed to collapse in manufacturing and refining demand even as medical oxygen rising
secondary_factors: Concern that healthcare gas demand would not offset weakness in industrial end-markets
store_description: Linde 7.0% drop looks mainly tied to a sharp downgrade in industrial demand expectations as U.S. manufacturing contracted and investors priced a deep pandemic recession. The cleanest explanation is that the market marked down gas suppliers for weaker manufacturing metals chemicals and energy volumes despite stronger medical oxygen demand.

primary_cause: Collapsing away-from-home beverage demand from restaurant theater and stadium closures. No new KO-specific release in prior 3 days but restaurants theaters and sports venues representing huge away-from-home channel were shut
secondary_factors: Overall April 1 market selloff. McDonald's trimmed U.S. menu on March 25 reinforcing foodservice channel pressure
store_description: Coke 4.8% decline was most likely driven by worsening expectations for foodservice and on-premise consumption as lockdowns shut restaurants movie theaters and sports venues. The market was increasingly pricing the channel exposure that would materially hurt second-quarter sales.

primary_cause: De-rating of premium-growth utility and renewables exposure under stressed capital markets. No strong NextEra-specific negative headline in prior 3 days. Falling equity values and macro stress make external financing and tax-equity funding harder
secondary_factors: Broad risk-off yield-sensitive selling and concern about project financing and tax equity
store_description: A 9.3% decline was too large to treat as a plain defensive-utility move. The best explanation is that investors aggressively sold the higher-multiple externally financed renewables story as market stress raised the cost of equity and funding just when the macro outlook was deteriorating sharply.

primary_cause: STOCK-SPECIFIC. Reuters reported hospitals were postponing elective surgeries as COVID spread exactly the setup that hurts da Vinci procedure volumes and system utilization. Collapse in elective surgery expectations
secondary_factors: April 1 macro selloff
store_description: Intuitive 7.5% decline was almost certainly driven by postponed elective surgeries which Reuters said hospitals were canceling to preserve beds staff and PPE. Since Intuitive is heavily tied to procedure volume and hospital capital spending that industry development was a clean stock-specific negative.

primary_cause: STOCK-SPECIFIC context. McDonald's said on March 25 it would temporarily remove some U.S. menu items to simplify operations during outbreak. Dine-in closures sweeping across states hurting traffic and franchisee economics
secondary_factors: Menu simplification signaled operating disruption. April 1 risk-off
store_description: McDonald's was not hit by one huge fresh headline but by accumulating evidence that the operating model was under stress. The March 25 menu cuts showed management simplifying kitchens for the crisis and widespread dine-in shutdowns made investors reassess same-store sales and franchisee cash flow.

primary_cause: Broad market de-risking and rotation not a stock-specific negative catalyst. No fresh Netflix-specific negative headline in prior 3 days. Netflix had been relative COVID winner
secondary_factors: Valuation sensitivity after relative outperformance during stay-at-home trading
store_description: Netflix 3.0% decline is one of the weakest moves in this batch which fits a market pulled everything down explanation more than a company-specific problem. No relevant March 29 to April 1 Netflix headline strong enough to justify calling it the driver.

primary_cause: Recession concerns around media and advertising plus debt sensitivity. No fresh AT&T-specific negative headline in prior 3 days. Obvious overhang was concern that WarnerMedia advertising theatrical and sports revenues would weaken while AT&T remained highly levered
secondary_factors: Market-wide selloff and uncertainty around WarnerMedia
store_description: AT&T 3.8% drop looks more like a macro and balance-sheet sensitivity trade than a reaction to a new press release. Investors were increasingly pricing the idea that the pandemic would pressure WarnerMedia revenues while AT&T still carried substantial debt making it less defensive than a plain telecom utility.

primary_cause: Multiple compression in enterprise software as recession risk rose. No meaningful ServiceNow-specific negative headline in prior 3 days. Selloff in high-multiple software on fears that enterprise IT spending and seat expansion could slow
secondary_factors: Broad market risk-off and concern about delayed enterprise projects
store_description: With no strong company-specific news in the window ServiceNow 4.7% decline is best explained by valuation and budget-risk concerns. On a day when investors were digesting sudden deterioration in payrolls and manufacturing richly valued enterprise software names were vulnerable to the idea that customers might delay implementations.

primary_cause: STOCK-SPECIFIC. IRS had extended federal tax filing deadline from April 15 to July 15. Pushed revenue recognition and seasonal tax demand later even if not permanently lost. Tax-deadline extension disrupting normal TurboTax seasonal revenue cadence
secondary_factors: Recession risk for small-business products. April 1 market selloff
store_description: Intuit had a more identifiable stock-specific issue than many names here: the federal filing deadline moved from April 15 to July 15 delaying the normal peak of tax-season revenue. That timing shock combined with rising small-business stress and a broad risk-off day likely explains the 5.2% decline.

primary_cause: Bank credit-loss fears. No fresh Wells-specific negative headline in prior 3 days. Worsening expectations for credit losses consumer delinquencies and NIM pressure as recession fears intensified
secondary_factors: Weak payroll and manufacturing data. Pressure on rates and profitability
store_description: Wells Fargo 7.4% decline fits a classic stressed-bank move as investors repriced unemployment consumer credit losses and commercial loan stress after the White House grim COVID forecast and weak U.S. economic data. No March 29 to April 1 Wells-specific corporate event stronger than that macro credit narrative.

primary_cause: STOCK-SPECIFIC. On March 30 Visa said transaction volumes fell in second half of March and cross-border travel-related spending was deteriorating rapidly with sharp week-on-week declines in travel restaurants entertainment and fuel
secondary_factors: April 1 market selloff
store_description: Visa 5.0% drop was driven by company-specific disclosure not just macro weakness. The March 30 statement quantified a rapid late-March deterioration in transaction volumes and especially cross-border travel spending which matters because cross-border is one of Visa most lucrative categories.

primary_cause: Rising expected credit losses and recession risk. No fresh USB-specific negative headline in prior 3 days. Like WFC and JPM traded off worsening recession and loan-loss expectations
secondary_factors: Sensitivity to small-business and consumer banking stress
store_description: U.S. Bancorp 7.3% decline looks sector-driven rather than company-driven. The combination of White House severe pandemic forecast and ADP 27K March job-loss print likely pushed investors to assume higher provisions weaker loan growth and more pressure on credit cards commercial real estate and small-business exposures.

primary_cause: Concern that global business disruption would outweigh parcel-demand positives near term. No fresh UPS-specific negative release in prior 3 days. E-commerce parcel demand rising but pandemic disrupting freight and customer activity broadly
secondary_factors: Uncertainty about customer mix small-business weakness and network costs
store_description: UPS modest 3.2% decline suggests the market saw it as less damaged than many cyclicals but still exposed to the recession. The most plausible explanation is investor worry that broad trade and business disruption especially from smaller commercial customers would pressure margins even as residential package volume improved.

primary_cause: Worsening rail-volume expectations especially intermodal and industrial freight. No fresh Union Pacific headline in prior 3 days. Later Reuters reporting confirmed first-quarter volume declines led by coal and intermodal and company withdrew 2020 outlook
secondary_factors: April 1 recession data and broad market selloff
store_description: Union Pacific 3.2% decline likely reflected the market pricing in lower freight volumes as the economy shut down. Reuters later reported first-quarter volumes fell 7% driven by coal and intermodal weakness and the company withdrew its 2020 outlook.
